title: Taifa of Zaragoza
capsule: The Taifa of Zaragoza (Arabic: طائفة سرقسطة, Saraqusta) was an independent Muslim principality in northeastern al-Andalus, established around 1013 after the collapse of the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba, governed first by the Tujibid dynasty and then by the Hudids from c. 1039. Under Ahmad al-Muqtadir (1046–1081/3) the taifa reached its greatest extent and served as a multilingual intellectual center — Arabic, Mozarabic, and Hebrew scholarship flourished there, with the philosopher Ibn Bajja (Avempace) among its most celebrated figures. The Almoravid confederation defeated and absorbed the taifa in May 1110; Alfonso I of Aragon captured Zaragoza itself in 1118, ending Muslim rule in the city permanently.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core territory of the Taifa of Zaragoza — the Ebro valley — is well-established; its fluctuating frontier zones with Christian kingdoms and rival taifas are less precisely mapped.
